topic_tag: an expressway and a mill town
passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. Its nearest exit lay nine miles away across the river, and the trucks that had crawled down the main street took the new road. The mill shipped by rail and kept its orders. In 1990 the planner found the families of 1958 behind most of the main street's counters, and its newest building was the 1951 post office. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: With traffic gone and nothing else changed (the mill's orders kept, the same families at the counters, no building newer than 1951), the expressway left the town held in its 1958 form: it "fossilized" it. "Drained" fails because the mill kept its orders and the families kept their stores; only through traffic left. "Engulfed" and "fragmented" both fail because the road ran across the river with its nearest exit nine miles off, so the city's spread could not reach the town and the road cut through none of it.

topic_tag: radio and a country's newspapers
passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations had no reporters and read the papers' stories aloud only after the papers were out. Advertisers moved their money to the stations, and by 1940 most papers had cut two thirds of their pages and every bureau outside their own city, filling the rest with that city's courts and council. They had voted together to cut the wire service to the one daily bulletin they could afford. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Losing their advertisers cost the papers two thirds of their pages, every outside bureau and most of their wire service, so they could no longer cover what they once had: radio "hamstrung" them. "Dethroned" fails because radio read the papers' stories only after the papers were out, so print still told the news first. "Homogenized" fails because the pages left went to each city's own courts and council. "Fractured" fails because the papers voted together on cutting the wire service.

topic_tag: an island in a strait
passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. Each summer, colliers from a mine across the ocean heaped coal behind the quay. All year the cities' steamships, which burned a ton of coal an hour, put in there on every voyage out and back, while sailing ships, which burned nothing, sailed straight through the strait. The coal was handled by two hundred dockworkers who lived in boardinghouses beside it. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Coal brought in each summer was kept behind the quay and drawn on all year by the cities' steamships on every voyage, so the island was their "depot." "Haven" fails because the steamships called on every voyage because their fuel was there, not to escape storms. "Gateway" fails because sailing ships went straight through without stopping. "Fortress" fails because the island's people were dockworkers handling coal.

topic_tag: a fallen log in a mountain stream
passage: In 1980 a storm dropped a two-hundred-year-old fir into a mountain stream, and its trunk, four feet thick, has lain there ever since. It came to rest along the current, parallel to the banks, and floods sweeping around it have scoured a pool ten feet deep in its shade. Each summer the pool holds hundreds of adult salmon, and fish tagged there turn up weeks later on gravel beds miles upstream. Seedlings sprout on its top each spring and are gone by winter, when the flood that deepens the pool runs over the trunk. After a decade of watching it, one ecologist called the log, above all, the valley's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Salmon tagged in the pool beside the log turn up weeks later on gravel beds miles upstream, so the log's pool is a resting stop on their journey: the valley's "hostel." "Hatchery" fails because the salmon spawn on those gravel beds upstream, not at the log. "Highway" fails because the log lies along the current, parallel to the banks, joining neither. "Garden" fails because the winter flood runs over the trunk and takes each year's seedlings.

topic_tag: a court ruling and a dockworkers' union
passage: In 1894 a court ruled on a strike by a port city's dockworkers' union, which then had four thousand members and a hall near the docks. The court let the union stand but barred it from enrolling any man hired after the ruling. Until the 1920s employers paid the union scale to every man on the docks rather than risk a walkout by its veterans. As those men retired, no one took their places in the union, and in 1931 its last local sold the hall. Writing fifty years later, one labor historian concluded that the ruling had, in effect, ______ the union.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Barred from enrolling new men, the union could only shrink as its veterans retired, until its last local sold the hall in 1931, so the ruling set it on a sure road to its end: it "doomed" the union. "Disbanded" fails because the union lasted thirty-seven more years. "Defanged" fails because employers paid every man the union scale rather than risk a walkout. "Divided" fails because the veterans remained a single body that employers feared would walk out together.

topic_tag: village retelling of a printed tale
passage: In 1650 a printed collection brought to a mountain region a long tale, set in a distant desert capital, of a merchant's son who outwits a robber king. The village versions recorded around 1900 still took about as long to tell as the printed text took to read. Tellers had reworked every line: the son's three tricks now came in rising order, the robber king's riddle rhymed on the names of the desert's three wells, and the surprise that the printed text gave away midway now fell on the last line. In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Every line had been reworked for effect (the tricks put in rising order, a rhyming riddle, the surprise moved to the last line), so retelling had "honed" the tale. "Distilled" and "fused" fail because a telling still took as long as reading the printed text, so the tale had neither been cut down nor joined to other material. "Domesticated" fails because the riddle rhymed on the names of the desert's wells, so the tale was still set in the desert.

topic_tag: an oasis on a caravan road
passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. By 1500 one family in the coastal city had bought every palm and well. Each autumn its stewards had the dates picked by tenant families and carried on the family's own camels to its warehouses on the coast, and passing caravans watered there free. In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: One coastal family owned every palm and well, and its stewards had tenants pick the dates and carry them to its own warehouses, so the oasis was a single owner's holding worked for profit: an "estate." "Emporium" fails because the whole crop went to the family's warehouses on the coast, so nothing was sold at the oasis. "Fairground" fails because the autumn crowd was the family's tenants at work. "Gatehouse" fails because caravans watered free.

topic_tag: stoats and a farmland hedge
passage: A single hawthorn hedge runs a mile east to west across open plowed fields between two oak woods, and voles burrow thickly in the bank beneath it. Each autumn young stoats leave the eastern wood to find territories, and nearly every adult trapped in the western wood had been collared as a kit in the east. Collars logged each young stoat at both ends of the hedge on the same night, and the bank's vole count was no lower after the autumn passage than before it. After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Stoats born in the eastern wood settled in the western one, passing through the hedge from end to end in a single night, so it was their "lane." "Inn" fails because a stoat logged at both ends on the same night did not stop there to rest. "Lair" fails because these stoats were born in one wood and settled in the other. "Larder" fails because the passing stoats took nothing from the bank's voles.

topic_tag: a flood after a drought
passage: In 1952, after three dry years, a river broke its banks and spread for five days across a broad valley, filling every side channel between its villages and their fields. It came down fast off bare slopes carrying coarse gray sand, which it dropped wherever the current slowed: in old stream channels, ditches and the low hollows the farmers had always plowed around. Rain returned that winter, and the next spring they plowed whole farms in straight furrows for the first time, the wheat in the old hollows coming up no thicker than elsewhere. One agronomist later argued that, for the farmers, the flood had above all ______ their fields.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The flood filled channels, ditches and hollows with sand, and the next spring farmers plowed whole farms in straight furrows, so it "leveled" their fields. "Irrigated" fails because rain returned that winter, so the flood's water gave the crop nothing the rain did not. "Nourished" fails because wheat on the new sand grew no thicker than elsewhere. "Marooned" fails because the sand filled the old channels and the farmers plowed every part of their farms.

topic_tag: a merchant's inherited estate in his account books
passage: In 1838 a merchant inherited an estate of farms and oak woods worked by hired hands, and his account books for the next twenty years survive. In 1841 and 1842 they record payments from a naval shipyard, entered load by load, together larger than ten years of the estate's profits. In 1843 he paid extra men to pull stumps and sow grass, and his regular hands' wages run on unchanged to 1858. From those books, one historian concluded that, above all, he had ______ the estate.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A naval shipyard paid him load by load, and afterward he hired men to pull stumps and sow grass, so he had sold the oaks: he had "logged" the estate. "Mortgaged" fails because money paid load by load by a shipyard is a buyer's price, not a loan. "Leased" fails because he himself paid the men who worked the land. "Liquidated" fails because he went on paying the estate's hands until 1858.

topic_tag: a parasitic worm in pond snails
passage: A parasitic worm that matures inside ducks infects half the snails in one pond, and for three years a biologist kept infected and uninfected snails in tanks and in a pen where ducks fed at the weed tips. Infected snails reached half the others' size and crept half as fast, while laying eggs weekly and living as long. Both kinds kept to the shaded weed bases in the pen, and a bacterium that swept the tanks took infected and uninfected snails in proportion to their numbers. From these results, she concluded that the worm had, above all, ______ its host.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Infected snails stayed small and slow but kept breeding and lived as long as the rest, so the worm drew on them steadily without killing them: it "milked" its host. "Neutered" fails because infected snails still laid eggs every week. "Manipulated" fails because infected snails stayed in the shaded weed bases with the others, away from the tips where ducks feed. "Immunized" fails because the bacterium took both kinds in proportion to their numbers.

topic_tag: a closely studied northern lake
passage: From 1950 to 1990, scientists studied one small, deep, cold lake in a northern forest more closely than any other lake in the region; its bottom mud reaches back to the last ice age. Its mud lies in yearly layers all the same thickness whatever the weather, one pale band each summer. Scientists at other lakes, whose own layers recorded rainfall but could not be counted reliably, dated those records by matching shared bands of volcanic ash against its exact count of years. In a history of that work, one scientist called the lake, for those four decades, above all the region's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Its layers come one a year, all alike, and scientists whose own lakes held the rainfall records set the dates of those records against its count, so the lake was the region's "metronome." "Ledger" fails because layers the same whatever the weather record nothing about any year, and the rainfall records were the other lakes'. "Microcosm" fails because scientists studied the other lakes directly and only borrowed this one's count. "Museum" fails because what others took from it was a count of years, a measure of time, not anything old kept to be seen.

topic_tag: two typewriter firms
passage: In 1904 a new firm began making typewriters in a country where one older company had sold nearly every machine for thirty years, and by 1914 the newcomer was outselling it. Its first machine sold for a third less than the older company's model, and repairmen found the older firm's spare parts fitted it throughout, down to the springs. In 1911 a court cleared the newcomer of stealing designs after hearing that its engineers had worked from machines bought in shops, and dealers stocked the two side by side. Reading both firms' records, one historian concluded that the newcomer had above all ______ its rival.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The older company's spare parts fitted the newcomer's cheaper machine throughout, and its engineers had worked from machines bought in shops, so the newcomer had "mimicked" its rival. "Infiltrated" fails because the design came from machines anyone could buy, not from inside the older firm. "Leapfrogged" fails because a machine that takes the rival's parts throughout is no step beyond it. "Isolated" fails because dealers stocked both machines side by side.

topic_tag: a buried silver hoard
passage: In 1987 a plowman near an old river landing turned up a clay pot buried around the year 900, holding some nine hundred silver coins and pieces of cut silver. The coins come from a dozen ports along the coast, and twelve different owners' marks are scratched into the cut silver. The pot lay in a boat shed at the landing that, a nearby abbey's chronicle records, a trading crew of twelve shared each winter. From its contents, one archaeologist concluded that the hoard had been, above all, its owners' ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Silver bearing twelve owners' marks, from the ports a crew of twelve traded at, sat in one pot in the shed they shared, so the hoard was money they had pooled: its owners' "kitty." "Insurance" fails because twelve owners' marks show many contributors, not one household's reserve. "Loot" fails because the silver carried the marks of the crew who owned it and came from the ports where they traded. "Inventory" fails because marked shares of money held in common are not a craftsman's stock.

topic_tag: a college farm station in a wheat district
passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. Each spring for forty years its staff sowed strains sent by breeders in other states in narrow strips beside the district's usual wheat. After five seasons the station printed each strain's harvests in the county paper, and the district's farmers took up the few strains that had held up. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Outside strains were grown beside the usual wheat for five seasons and farmers adopted only the ones that held up, so the station was where new wheat was tried first: a "testbed." "Wellspring" fails because the strains were bred in other states; the station sorted them but originated nothing. "Yardstick" fails because the fixed standard in the strips was the district's usual wheat, while the station's own plantings changed with every batch. "Stopgap" fails because the trials ran every spring for forty years, a standing program rather than cover for the closed merchant until trade returned.

topic_tag: a dawn auction rule at a fishing port
passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. A village four miles down the coast, where crews could still sell to any buyer at any hour, built a new quay in 1932. Within two years the city's fish merchants had moved their stalls there, the boats followed them, and carts carried each catch up the coast road to the same city shops as before. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The city's merchants and boats moved to the village quay while the same city shops kept getting their fish by cart, so the rule "uprooted" the market: the whole market went on, in another place. "Stifled" fails because the city's shops were supplied as before, so the city's fish market lost its site, not its trade. "Saturated" fails because the boats landed at the village, so no fish reached the city's quay to glut it. "Steadied" fails because a market whose merchants, boats and quay all moved within two years was overturned, not settled.

topic_tag: a volcanic island two decades after an eruption
passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Landing twenty years later, surveyors found bare rock, scored with grooves running downhill, where the farms and the village had been, and fishermen offshore still snagged roof beams in their nets. The tide still reached the old mark cut in the quay's bedrock, and the island's one stream still ran to the harbor down its old gully. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Bare rock grooved downhill where farms and houses stood, with their beams now in the sea, shows that the eruption dragged the surface off: it "scoured" the island. "Smothered" fails because the rock was left bare, with nothing lying over it. "Submerged" fails because the tide still reaches the old mark in the quay's bedrock, so the beams were carried into the sea while the land stayed up. "Tilted" fails because the stream still runs down its old gully, which tipped ground would have turned aside.

topic_tag: a mountain lake above orchards and trout ponds
passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. The lake lies on porous limestone, and water seeps through its floor into caverns that open, miles away, as springs in another valley. Below the outlet the river runs half as wide as above the lake, and in dry summers its bed lies bare; the seepage keeps the lake shallow, so in August the ponds draw on wells. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Water seeps through the lake's limestone floor into caverns that empty into another valley, so the river loses half its water there: the lake is a "sink." "Valve" fails because the water missing in dry summers is not held for later; it comes out as springs in another valley. "Tributary" fails because the river leaves the lake half as wide. "Thermostat" fails because the seepage keeps the lake shallow, and the ponds must turn to wells in August.

topic_tag: restoring a sixteenth-century altarpiece
passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. Because the museum planned a ten-city tour and the three panels together weighed four hundred pounds, the restorers faced the paint with tissue and shaved the sound oak away from behind it. On tour the altarpiece weighed thirty pounds, its back now canvas stretched on aluminum, and crowds saw the same smoke-browned saints they had known in the church. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The oak was shaved away from behind the paint and the altarpiece's back is now canvas on aluminum, so the restorers "transferred" it to a new support. "Stabilized" fails because the oak was sound; it was removed to save weight for a tour, not to arrest any decay. "Scrubbed" fails because the saints were still smoke-browned, so nothing was cleaned. "Uncovered" fails because the crowds saw the same saints they had always known, so nothing hidden came into view.

topic_tag: a giant planet in a model planetary system
passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, icy bodies that drifted near it left on long, stretched paths, three of every four outward and clean out of the system, the fourth inward across the rocky planets' orbits. Within a hundred million years the belt held half as many bodies as in the run without the giant. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Icy bodies passing near the giant were flung onto stretched paths, most out of the system, so the giant acted as the system's "slingshot." "Umbrella" fails because a quarter of the flung bodies were sent inward across the rocky planets' orbits, so the giant aimed bodies at the inner planets rather than shielding them. "Shepherd" fails because the belt lost half its bodies instead of being kept in bounds. "Tether" fails because the bodies near the giant left on long paths rather than being held in place.

topic_tag: early records of a mountain region's ballads
passage: Between 1925 and 1935 a record company sent engineers into a mountain region to record its fiddlers and ballad singers, and it sold the records by the thousand. The engineers recorded in farmhouse kitchens, taking each fiddle and voice as they found it, and sold most records at the general stores of the mountain towns. A record side held three minutes, and the young people who learned the ballads from those records knew a twenty-verse ballad by its first five or six verses, which they sang at every weekend dance. Looking back in 1970, one folklorist argued that the records had ______ the region's songs.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A three-minute side held only the first few verses, and the young learned only those, so the records "stripped" the ballads of most of their verses. "Smoothed" fails because the engineers took each fiddle and voice as they found it in farmhouse kitchens. "Transplanted" fails because the records sold in the region's own mountain towns, so the songs stayed where they were. "Silenced" fails because the young people sang the songs at every weekend dance.

topic_tag: a foreign carmaker's first plant in a country
passage: In 1965 a carmaker from abroad opened a plant outside a port city, on a site its board had chosen after two years of study. The company had sold cars in the country through an importer since 1930, and the plant's long sheds took in the cars that importer had kept on the docks, as many as twenty thousand shipped whole from abroad, with parts for every model. Dealers drew on them as orders came, and the plant's three hundred local workers spent their days washing, checking and loading cars onto trains. In a history of the company, one economist called the plant, above all, its ______ in the country.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The sheds took in thousands of imported cars and parts that dealers drew on as orders came, so the plant was the company's "warehouse." "Toehold" fails because the company had sold cars in the country since 1930, so the plant took over an established trade rather than opening one. "Schoolhouse" fails because its workers spent their days washing, checking and loading finished cars, so it taught no one to build them. "Showroom" fails because sheds holding up to twenty thousand cars are built for stock, not for visitors.

topic_tag: gravel bar across a bay mouth
passage: A gravel bar a mile long runs from the southern shore of a bay toward an island at the bay's mouth. At the lowest tides its crest lies dry from the shore to the island for two hours, and at high water eight feet covers it from end to end. The town's sheep graze the island's pasture from May to October. The fishing fleet sails over the bar at any point along its length on the flood, and winters on the beach like every fleet on that coast. One historian of the bay's fishing town wrote that the bar had served the town above all as its ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The crest lies dry from the shore to the island at low tide, and the town's sheep spend each summer on the island, so the bar is the town's "causeway" to its pasture. "Breakwater" fails because the fleet still winters on the beach like boats on the open coast. "Barricade" fails because eight feet of water covers the bar at high tide. "Chokepoint" fails because the fleet can cross anywhere along the bar.

topic_tag: gale and a sand spit
passage: A sand spit four miles long curves across a lagoon's mouth, with a lighthouse near its hooked tip and a road along its crest. In 1953 a three-day gale drove waves over the crest. When the water fell, the road ran over cobbles that had lain beneath the crest's sand. The keeper's cart to town ran as usual, boats still moored behind the hook, and the lagoon-side boathouses stood at the water's edge as before. In the next twenty winters the spit lost less ground than in any twenty on record. Comparing surveys made before and after that winter, one geologist concluded that the gale had ______ the spit.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The gale stripped the crest's sand down to a bed of cobbles, and afterward the spit wore away more slowly than ever before, so the gale had "armored" it. "Cleaved" fails because the keeper's cart still ran along the crest to town. "Blunted" fails because boats still moored behind the hook. "Broadened" fails because the lagoon-side boathouses still stood at the water's edge.

topic_tag: a city council's granary
passage: In 1590 the council of a river city built a stone granary on its market square, large enough to hold a year's grain for every household. The lords of the villages around it often quarreled with the city over its barge tolls. Each autumn the council bought every village's surplus at harvest prices, and each spring it shipped the grain downriver to whichever port paid most, in famine years as in good. The city raised no hearth tax except in the two years a war closed the river. One economic historian has argued that for two centuries the granary served above all as the city's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The council bought at harvest prices and sold to whichever port paid most, and the city needed a hearth tax only in the two years war stopped the shipments, so the granary's trade paid the city's way: it was the city's "coffer." "Ballast" fails because the grain was shipped downriver and never reached the city's own market. "Backstop" fails because it was shipped out even in famine years. "Cudgel" fails because the council bought from every village alike, quarrel or no quarrel, and sold on price alone.

topic_tag: an island in a valley river
passage: A rocky island a quarter mile long lies in the middle of a wide river where it crosses a farming valley. Gravel shallows run out to it from both banks, where the current runs fastest. In late summer the valley's harvest carts reach the market town on the far bank by way of the island. Raiders coming downriver in 1640 burned the island's barns along with the valley's, and every spring flood leaves a line of driftwood across its crown. In a history of the valley, one historian called the island, above all, the valley's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Gravel shallows reach the island from both banks, and the harvest carts get to the market town on the far bank by way of it, so it is the valley's "crossing." "Anchorage" fails because the current runs fastest over those shallows, so no barge can lie there. "Citadel" fails because raiders burned the island's barns with everyone else's. "Ark" fails because spring floods leave driftwood across its crown.

topic_tag: a kiln firing and a glaze
passage: A potter fired a batch of white bowls painted with blue brushwork under a clear glaze. The brushwork could be made out only faintly, and the bowls' thin rims, which had glowed when held up to a window, now let no light through. The white ground of each bowl looked whiter than before, the glaze was as smooth as glass under a fingertip, and tea left in the bowls overnight washed out without a trace. In her notes on the batch, the potter concluded that the firing had ______ the glaze.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The glaze stopped letting light through and dimmed the brushwork while the white ground looked whiter, so it had turned pale and opaque: the firing had "clouded" it. "Blackened" fails because the bowls looked whiter, not darker. "Blistered" fails because the glaze was as smooth as glass. "Cracked" fails because tea washed out without a trace.

topic_tag: a spring flood on salted valley fields
passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water, clear snowmelt that had crossed the upland meadows, stood nine days and sank through the sandy ground into the ditches below. Afterward cattle grazed the old stubble and the fallow strips along the ditches, which fed them no better than in other years. That summer the same seed wheat that had always yielded half as much there as on the upper slopes matched them. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Clear water stood for nine days on salt-crusted fields and drained down through sandy ground, after which the same wheat grew as well as on the upper slopes, so the flood "rinsed" the salt out of the lower fields. "Reseeded" fails because the fallow strips fed the cattle no better than usual. "Replenished" fails because clear snowmelt adds no silt, and "plowed" fails because the old stubble was still there to graze.

topic_tag: a hill temple and a city temple
passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. A lord of the northern hills built it, and its monks came from a coastal order and kept that order's rule. He set its festival for the same spring week as the city's, beneath a gate carved taller than the city temple's. Within ten years the city's festival tolls had fallen by half. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A hill lord built the temple with monks of another order, set its festival for the city's own spring week, and within ten years the city's festival tolls had fallen by half, so it was the city temple's "rival". "Offshoot" fails because its monks came from a coastal order with its own rule. "Replica" fails because its gate was carved taller than the city temple's, and "precursor" fails because its festival was timed against a city festival already being held.

topic_tag: winter sea ice in a northern bay
passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there is frozen fast to the shore, thick and snow-covered, so the water beneath stays dark and almost nothing grows there. Young cod spend the winter in crevices on its underside, swimming out at night to feed in open water past its edge. The seabirds that hunt them find fish by sight, and at the bay's mouth, where no ice forms, they take most of the young cod wintering there. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Young cod hide in crevices under the dark ice by day, and the seabirds that hunt by sight take most of the young cod only at the ice-free mouth of the bay, so the ice serves as the cod's "roof". "Pantry" fails because almost nothing grows under the thick, snowy ice and the cod swim out past its edge to feed. "Raft" fails because the ice is frozen fast to the shore and carries nothing, and "perch" fails because the cod live under the ice, not on it.

topic_tag: a summer drought on a trout river
passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. Its springs held up, and in the eighth week the mill where the river meets the lake still turned its wheel at its usual summer speed. Along the shallow, treeless lower miles, biologists counted thousands of dead trout, many carrying tags put on near the springs that spring. In the shaded upper miles near the cold springs, the trout lived. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The river kept its usual flow, yet trout died by the thousands in the shallow, treeless lower miles while they lived in the shaded miles near the cold springs, so the drought "overheated" the river. "Pooled" fails because tagged trout traveled from the springs downstream. "Pinched" fails because the mill turned at its usual speed, and "parched" fails because the springs held up.

topic_tag: a copper mountain after mining
passage: For eighty years after 1890, companies mined copper from a mountain above a valley town, until the last mine closed in 1972. The ore lay in a dozen scattered pockets near the surface, and for eighty years the company's miners worked them in daylight, each pocket becoming a crater, some a quarter mile across, the deepest now holding rainwater. Between them the slopes keep their old forest, and the mountain still keeps the morning sun off the town until nine. A trout hatchery below it still raises its fish in water piped from the mountain's streams. Surveying the mountain in 1980, one geologist wrote that mining had ______ it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A dozen scattered pockets were each dug out in daylight into craters, some a quarter mile across, with old forest between them, so mining had "pitted" the mountain. "Riddled" fails because the miners worked from the surface, not through tunnels. "Razed" fails because the mountain still shades the town until nine, and "poisoned" fails because a trout hatchery still uses its water.

topic_tag: a century of a small country's wheat duty
passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. Governments of the farm party raised the rate and governments of the city party cut it, and the two held office by turns for the whole century. Two of the rises came in years of record wheat prices. In 1950 the rate stood within a cent of its first level, while the neighboring countries kept their 1850 duties throughout. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The duty rose under one party and fell under the other as they traded office, ending within a cent of where it began, so it was a "pendulum". "Ratchet" fails because the duty came back to its starting level. "Regulator" fails because two rises came in years of record prices, and "pacemaker" fails because the neighbors kept their 1850 duties throughout.

topic_tag: a city library under wartime occupation
passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. Staff who broke the authority's seals on its doors in 1945 had first to carry out crates of the army's own files stacked in the reading rooms. The forty of the library's authors on the authority's banned list of 1941 still stood on the shelves, the bound newspapers lay under five years of dust, and the rare-book room's own seal bore the date 1940. In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The doors were sealed until 1945, the reading rooms were used to store army files, and inside even the banned authors, the bound newspapers and the sealed rare-book room were untouched, so the occupation had "padlocked" the library. "Purged" fails because the banned authors still stood on the shelves. "Pulped" fails because the bound newspapers lay under five years of dust, and "plundered" fails because the rare-book room's seal of 1940 was unbroken.
